title: Upbeat alternatives to global climate defeatism
text:
Upbeat alternatives to global climate defeatism
The recent COP31 summit ended without the customary joint declaration. But, responding to citizen demands, countries are pursuing coalitions and technologies in a quest for autonomy and affordability.
Just a couple of weeks ago, a Monitor editorial referred to “a degree of pessimism” pervading November’s COP31 global climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. At the same time, it noted, a range of private funding solutions are helping “catalyze global efforts,” despite the disagreements among governments.
After the summit ended Sunday without a consensus declaration, pessimism might seem justified. Major oil-producing nations such as Russia and Saudi Arabia objected to any reference to a “transition away from fossil fuels” – a phrase first included in a 2023 COP (Conference of the Parties) meeting hosted in Dubai – at which point some 90 countries refused to sign on. (The United States, the world’s largest oil producer, did not participate in this year’s meeting.)
But several observers reject the view that lack of a declaration signals a failure of global progress on climate issues.
“What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards,” two Australian academics wrote in The Conversation a few days ago. This could involve more nations working together in other forums or coalitions, such as the April conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels held in Colombia, which was attended by 57 countries.
“Emerging from the sidelines of COP is a new type of climate diplomacy” in which smaller groups of countries “are clubbing together to agree to steps,” according to Carbon Brief, a specialist energy and climate outlet.
Regardless of international diplomatic hurdles, for many national governments the debate is moving away from arguments about the accuracy or otherwise of climate projections and alleged fearmongering by environmentalists. Instead, it’s taking into account national economic priorities and citizens’ demands for energy that is more affordable and less polluting. Across the European Union’s 27 member nations, for instance, 87% of 23,000 people surveyed “wanted the shift to low carbon energy to be prioritised,” according to an exclusive Nov. 5 Reuters report. Halfway around the world, a nationwide survey in the Philippines found 93% of Filipinos calling for acceleration of the transition to solar energy.
Rather than succumbing to gloom over the oil shocks from the U.S. war with Iran, governments are absorbing lessons of self-sufficiency and energy independence from current geopolitics.
“Many are treating the new low-carbon economy as a major growth and development opportunity,” observed the London-based think tank Chatham House. And, perhaps surprisingly, China, the world’s largest emitter of greenhouse gases, is playing a key role in making this possible. At home, it “has installed more [solar power] capacity in the past four years than every other nation combined,” The Financial Times reported Nov. 20, and accounted “for almost 70 per cent of the world’s growth in wind capacity last year.”
More broadly, China’s production of low-carbon technologies is also helping other nations transition to more affordable and cleaner energy for their citizens. One 2026 study estimated that China’s exports of items such as solar panels, batteries, and electric cars are on track to cut global CO2 emissions by an amount equivalent to Brazil’s annual rate.
“The gridlock in negotiations matters less and less to the energy transition, which now has its own momentum,” according to ODI Global, a think tank with offices in London, Brussels, and Washington. Nations across Europe, Africa, and Asia, it points out, “are embracing the opportunity to reduce their dependence on unreliable trade partners, vulnerable supply chains and centralised generation infrastructure.”
This transition might not be easy or quick, but it points to an ability and willingness to adapt diplomacy and coalition-building to address shared goals.
